blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper that introduces Nemo, a system for debugging distributed protocols by suggesting fixes at the protocol level. Adrian Colyer highlights three key aspects: (1) Nemo's ability to identify and propose corrections for protocol-level issues, such as premature acknowledgments leading to state loss, (2) the use of Dedalus, a temporal logic programming language based on Datalog, which offers a novel paradigm for reasoning about distributed systems, and (3) the research strategy of starting with an idealized model with perfect information before generalizing to real-world scenarios. The paper also addresses the challenge of debugging errors of omission in distributed systems, where oversights in protocol design lead to vulnerabilities. Nemo leverages provenance graphs to debug both errors of commission and omission, using differential provenance to pinpoint causes of failures and suggest corrections.
paper_title: Fixed it for you: protocol repair using lineage graphs
paper_abstract: Distributed systems are difficult to program and near impossible to debug. Existing tools that focus on single-node computation are poorly-suited to diagnose errors that involve the interaction of many machines over time. The database notion of provenance would appear to be a better fit for answering the sort of cause-and-effect questions that arise during debugging, but existing provenance-based approaches target only a narrow set of debugging scenarios. In this paper, we explore the limits of provenance-based debugging. We propose a simple query language to express common debugging questions as expressions over provenance graphs capturing traces of distributed executions. When programs and their correctness properties are written in the same highlevel declarative language, we can go a step further than highlighting errors by often generating repairs for distributed programs. We validate our prototype debugger, Nemo, on six protocols from our taxonomy of 52 real-world distributed bugs, either generating repair rules or pointing the programmer to root causes.
